uncited: The method computes a weighted sum of four loss components, each measuring a different aspect of the difference between the rendered image and the ground truth image.

- Images are treated as tensors of floating-point values, typically normalized to $[0, 1]$ or $[-1, 1]$ depending on the specific implementation of the underlying metrics (LPIPS typically expects normalized inputs).
- $\mathcal{L}_{\textrm{L1}}$ is the per-pixel L1 norm (mean absolute error) between $I_{render}$ and $I_{gt}$.
- $\mathcal{L}_{\textrm{L2}}$ is the per-pixel L2 norm (mean squared error) between $I_{render}$ and $I_{gt}$.
This is typically computed as $1 - \text{MS-SSIM}(I_{render}, I_{gt})$, where MS-SSIM evaluates structural similarity at multiple resolutions.
It measures perceptual distance by comparing features extracted from a pretrained deep neural network.
The weights control the relative importance of each term.
- **Time Complexity:** The computational cost is dominated by the LPIPS calculation, which requires forward passes through a pretrained deep neural network (AlexNet or VGG).
MS-SSIM also adds overhead due to multi-scale decomposition.
- **Memory Complexity:** Requires storing the intermediate feature maps for the LPIPS network and the multi-scale representations for MS-SSIM during the forward pass.
The inclusion of LPIPS increases training time significantly compared to pixel-only losses.
- **When to use:** When perceptual quality is prioritized over raw pixel-wise accuracy and computational efficiency is secondary to visual fidelity in 3D Gaussian Splatting optimization.
